title: Strings
summary: A string is text inside quote marks. JavaScript can join strings and find or change parts of them.
introduction: A string is text inside quote marks. JavaScript can join strings and find or change parts of them. Make a greeting from a name. Then count its letters, search for a word and try a simple text change.
learningObjectives: Write strings with single, double and backtick quotes and embed values in template literals
Access characters and the length of a string and explain immutability
Search strings with includes, startsWith, indexOf and slice
Transform text with trim, split, join, replace and padStart

blocks.text: Three ways to write a string

Single and double quotes are equivalent; pick one style and stay with it. A quote inside the string either needs the other kind of quote around the string or a backslash **escape** (`\'`, `\"`). Backticks create a **template literal**, which can span lines and embed any expression with `${...}`; it is the most readable way to build text from values.

blocks.content:
It's a single-quoted string
She said "hi"
Hello, Ada! 2 + 2 = 4
first line
second line

blocks.text: Inside quotes, a backslash starts an **escape sequence**: `\n` begins a new line, `\t` inserts a tab and `\\` is a literal backslash. Template literals rarely need them, because you can simply press Enter for a new line, but you will meet escape sequences in JSON data and in code written before template literals existed.

`length` counts characters, square brackets or `at()` read one character by position (starting at `0`), and methods such as `toUpperCase` produce a transformed copy. That last point is the key fact about strings: they are **immutable**. No method changes the original; each returns a new string, which you must store if you want to keep it.

blocks.title: Calling a method without using the result
blocks.text: `name.trim();` on its own does nothing useful: the trimmed string is created and thrown away. Write `name = name.trim();` or `const clean = name.trim();`. The same applies to every string method, because none of them modifies the string it is called on.

`includes`, `startsWith` and `endsWith` answer yes/no questions. `indexOf` returns the position of the first match, or `-1` when there is none. `slice(start, end)` extracts the characters from `start` up to but not including `end`; a negative `start` counts from the end. All searches are case-sensitive, so lower-case both sides when case should not matter.

blocks.content:
true
true
false
4
-1
quick
dog
true

blocks.text: `trim` removes whitespace from both ends, which you should do to every value typed by a user. `split` breaks a string into an array at a separator and `join` does the reverse. `replace` changes only the first match of a string pattern, `replaceAll` changes every one. `repeat` and `padStart` help with formatting: repeating a character or padding a number with leading zeros.

Most text tasks are a chain of these methods. `initials` splits a full name into words, takes the first letter of each and joins them; `countVowels` loops over the characters of a lower-cased string and checks membership with `includes`.

`===` compares strings character by character, so `"Ada" === "ada"` is false. For user-facing sorting use `localeCompare`, which understands accents and case the way people expect, instead of `<` and `>`, which compare raw character codes and put every capital letter before every lower-case one.

blocks.content:
false
true
false
-1
Apple, fig, pear

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Write `slugify(title)` that turns `"Hello Wide World"` into `"hello-wide-world"` using `trim`, `toLowerCase`, `split` and `join`. Then extend it to collapse several spaces by filtering out empty parts.

questions.question: What does `"hello".slice(1, 3)` return?
questions.explanation: slice starts at index 1 ("e") and stops before index 3, so it returns the two characters "el".

questions.question: `text.replace("a", "o")` replaces every "a" in the string.
questions.explanation: With a string pattern, replace changes only the first match. Use replaceAll, or a regular expression with the g flag, to change every occurrence.
